title.narrative: LPI Ethiopia Programme 2023 to 2026 - Sowing the Seeds of Peace in Ethiopia
LPI Ethiopia Programme 2023 to 2026 - Sowing the Seeds of Peace in Ethiopia

description.narrative:
Life & Peace Institute (LPI) har varit en långvarig partner till Sverige i dess globala, regionala och olika bilaterala strategier. LPI Addis Abeba Office övervakar både för Afrikas horn-programmet (HARP) och Etiopien-programmet.
LPI har stött lokalt drivna fredsbyggande initiativ i Etiopien sedan 1991 genom partnerskap med samhällen inklusive traditionella ledare och civilsamhällesorganisationer. Denna intervention ses som den andra fasen av LPI Etiopienprogram som stöddes av Sverige genom sin bilaterala strategi från 2017 till 2022.
Syftet med denna intervention är att vårda och upprätthålla civilsamhällesledda, inkluderande fredsbyggande processer för förebyggande, hantering och lösning av konflikter med fredliga medel i Etiopien.
Den totala budgeten som förväntas för att genomföra LPI Etiopienprogram under fyra år (2023 – 2026) är 75,7 MSEK och Sveriges bidrag kommer att vara totalt 44 MSEK under fyra år med start april 2023.

The Life & Peace Institute (LPI) has been a long-time partner to Sweden in its Global, regional and various bilateral strategies. LPI Addis Ababa Office oversees both for the Horn of Africa Programme (HARP) and the Ethiopia Programme.
LPI has supported locally driven peace building initiatives in Ethiopia since 1991 through partnerships with communities including traditional leaders and civil society organisations. This intervention is seen as the second phase of LPI’s Ethiopia Programme that was supported by Sweden through its bilateral strategy from 2017 until 2022.
The objective of this intervention is to nurture and sustain civil society-led, inclusive peace building processes for prevention, management and resolution of conflicts by peaceful means in Ethiopia.
The total budget expected for implementing the LPI’s Ethiopia Programme over four years (2023 – 2026) is 75.7 MSEK and Sweden's contribution will be a total of 44 MSEK for four years starting April 2023.

The overall objective of the programme is:
Nurture and sustain civil society-led, inclusive peacebuilding processes for prevention, management and resolution of conflicts by peaceful means in Ethiopia.
Objective 1: The role of Ethiopian peacebuilding CSOs in dialogue and reconciliation efforts at the national, regional and community levels is enhanced.?
Objective 2: Stakeholders in and around the universities take collaborative action to promote peaceful and inclusive campuses and communities.?
Objective 3: Increased collective actions to address causes/drivers of conflict within and between communities sustainably.?
Objective 4: Relevant policy stakeholders?take actions that support inclusive dialogue and,?reconciliation processes and peace building in Ethiopia.?

sector.narrative: Civilian peace-building, conflict prevention and resolution

description.narrative:
Pillar - one
- Improved conflict analysis practices: Training on the Resilience in Conflict Analysis Toolkit (RCAT) was provided to 23 CSOs, leading to a shift from grievancefocused analysis to more comprehensive, resilience and solutionoriented approaches. Following the training, CSOs began integrating and applying the tools directly in their programming and community dialogue work.
- Small grants to emerging CSOs: Eight emerging CSOs received small grants and applied conflict analysis training to design and implement locally tailored interventions across ten regions, reaching thousands of community members.
- Strengthened resource mobilization capacity: Resource mobilization and financial sustainability training were provided to around 23 CSOs, improving their ability to plan and manage financial sustainability more strategically. Following the training, seven CSOs developed their firstever resource mobilization strategies, while most others revised existing ones. Three CSOs also successfully accessed new funding from donors including the EU, Austrian Embassy, and Canadian Embassy.
- Enhanced CSO coordination and policy influence: LPI supported platforms that convened around 3040 CSOs to share experiences, learn, and collaborate. Through this coordination, CSOs moved from fragmented efforts to more strategic, collective advocacy, and a new network was formed that is already actively convening CSOs despite not yet being formally registered. Coordinated CSO input to the Ministry of Justice contributed to the removal of some restrictive provisions in the controversial draft CSO law.
Pillar - Two
Strengthened student leadership and conflict management capacity: Training in dialogue facilitation, conflict analysis, and leadership was provided to 50 student leaders and moderators at Hawassa and Mekelle universities. As a result, students improved their ability to facilitate dialogue on sensitive issues such as ethnicity, mediate peer conflicts, and adopt more inclusive, dialoguecentered leadership practices.
Improved trust and intergroup relationships among students in campuses: Trained students facilitated over 200 dialogue sessions involving over 250 students from diverse ethnic and religious backgrounds. These sessions enabled students to move from mistrust and isolation toward empathy, friendship, and collaboration, contributing to stronger peer relationships and an increased sense of safety and belonging on campus.
Increased student-led peace initiatives and collective action: Dialogue participants (250 students) translated learning into practical action through campus peace initiatives, including peer-support activities, recreation events, skills-sharing workshops, and peace promotion campaigns. These campus-wide peace actions engaged more than 2,900 students, university staff, and administrators in promoting peaceful coexistence and celebrating diversity.
Institutionalized universitycommunity dialogue platforms: The dialogue processes started since the start of the programm in 2023 culminated during the reporting period with the establishment of structured platforms between universities and surrounding communities, transforming previously ad hoc and crisisdriven interactions into regular, formalized engagement. This led to jointly agreed action plans and the signing of commitment statements that provided a foundation for sustained collaboration and conflict resolution beyond the project period.
Improved campuscommunity security and reduced crime rates: Joint dialogue and collaboration between universities and surrounding communities contributed to the recovery of stolen university assets and a reduction in crime rates in surrounding areas, as reported by local authorities. These outcomes reflect improved trust, coordination, and shared responsibility between universities and communities.
Pillar - Three
Strengthened community capacity for dialogue and conflict transformation: A total of 48 community members were trained in conflict analysis and dialogue facilitation. They subsequently facilitated 296 community dialogue sessions across 20 conflicts affected kebeles in Dire Dawa, Shashemene, Bale Goba and Harar engaging 931 community members in analyzing conflict drivers and identifying locally led peacebuilding solutions. The dialogues helped communities develop a more shared understanding of the underlying causes of local conflicts beyond immediate triggers.
Enhanced community collective action through reconciliation: Dialogue processes contributed to the reconciliation of long-standing interpersonal, interreligious, and community disputes that had remained unresolved for years.
Communities translated dialogue into collective peace action: Dialogue processes generated more than 20 community-led peace actions, including peace walks, cultural festivals, reconciliation events, awareness campaigns, mediation initiatives, and community peace education activities.
Sustainable local peace infrastructures established: The programme established community peace committees, reconciliation committees, school peace clubs, and peace ambassador networks to strengthen local capacity for conflict prevention and mediation beyond the project period. In Dire Dawa, the first Community Mediation Centre was established in partnership with local authorities, providing a locally owned mechanism for resolving disputes outside the formal justice system. In addition, school peace clubs introduced peer mediation and peace education in 13 secondary schools, strengthening youth engagement in peacebuilding and creating networks for continued collaboration.
Pillar Four
Strengthened civil society influence and participation in national peace processes: Civil society engagement in the National Dialogue process became more structured, coordinated, and influential through strengthened partnerships between ECSOC, CSOs, and the National Dialogue Commission (NDC). Joint committees, quarterly review platforms, and regular consultation mechanisms enabled CSOs to provide coordinated input and monitor dialogue processes more effectively.
Research and scholarly evidence informed National Dialogue and transitional justice: LPI-supported research and dialogue processes involving historians and scholars from Ethiopian universities generated evidence-based inputs for the National Dialogue Commission on contentious historical and governance issues. To strengthen civil society engagement in transitional justice, LPI supported the establishment of a CSO Transitional Justice Reference Group, providing a platform for coordination, information sharing, and collective engagement. Training on human rights documentation, survivor protection, and victim-centred approaches further strengthened CSOs' capacity to contribute to future transitional justice processes.
Advanced the Youth, Peace and Security (YPS) agenda: LPI contributed to the development of Ethiopias first Youth, Peace and Security National Action Plan. It convened a national youth forum with 250 participants across Ethiopia who contributed to the action plan, engaged in dialogue on peace and governance issues and jointly developed the Addis Declaration on Peace. The declaration was formally submitted to the Ministry of Women and Social Affairs (MoWSA).
Contributed to policy dialogue and preventive diplomacy: LPI provided policy analysis and conflict assessments that informed the international community about the conflict dynamics in Tigray and Ethiopia-Eritrea relations during a period of heightened tension. Through engagement with Nordic and other international partners, LPI contributed to identifying opportunities for dialogue, preventive diplomacy, and conflict prevention.
